chapter_theme: Eating flesh is incompatible with அருள், and the chapter argues this like a debate, answering those who say that intent is what matters and those who say that the guilt lies only with the killer. It ends by exalting the one who neither kills nor eats.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as refuting two opponents: those who claim flesh-eating doesn't harm அருள் if one means no harm (251-253), and those who claim the sin of killing stays with the killer (254-256). Then come flesh's repulsiveness (257) and the height of abstaining (258-260).

251.reading: How can one who eats another's flesh to swell his own hold to அருள்?
251.nuance: ஊன் appears on both sides, so the eater is flesh too and the act is flesh feeding flesh. Parimelazhagar adds that fattening the body is itself useless, so the cruelty buys nothing.

252.reading: Holding wealth isn't for those who don't guard it, and likewise holding அருள் isn't for those who eat flesh.
252.nuance: ஆட்சி, holding and using, is the operative word: compassion is a possession that lapses through neglect. For Parimelazhagar the verse answers those who say a flesh-eater who wishes no creature harm hasn't compromised அருள்.

positions.position: The verse rebuts the claim that good intention makes flesh-eating harmless to அருள்.
positions.quote: ஊன் தின்றாராயினும் உயிர்கட்கு ஒரு தீங்கும் நினையாதார்க்கு அருள் ஆள்தற்கு இழுக்கு இல்லை என்பாரை மறுத்து,

253.reading: The mind of one who has relished another creature's body doesn't incline to good, like the heart of one holding a weapon.
253.nuance: The argument concerns attention rather than guilt: what the hand holds, or the tongue relishes, takes over the mind. சுவை matters here, since the verse speaks of savouring and not merely of eating.

254.reading: If asked what is அருள் and what isn't, it comes down to not killing and killing; eating that flesh is not பொருள்.

positions.position: அருள் is not killing and its opposite is killing, and பொருள் here means virtue, so eating is sin. He also reports another division of the words.
Non-அருள் is destroying the vow of not killing, and பொருள் means gain, so eating harms அருள் and gets one nothing.

255.reading: The standing of life lies in not eating flesh; if one eats, hell doesn't open its mouth.
255.nuance: The image is of a mouth that has swallowed and won't open to release. Parimelazhagar offers a population argument for உயிர்நிலை: creatures that are eaten dwindle while others multiply. Kalaignar takes அளறு as a mud pit, not the hell of the older commentators.

256.reading: If the world didn't kill for the sake of eating, nobody would bring flesh for the sake of a price.
256.nuance: This is a demand-and-supply argument. The buyer who says he killed nothing is told that his purchase causes the killing. Parimelazhagar formalizes the reply as inference by necessary implication.

positions.position: It answers those who ask what fault there is in buying and eating without having killed.
positions.quote: கொன்று தின்னாது விலைக்குக் கொண்டு தின்பார்க்குக் குற்றமென்னை யென்றார்க்கு , அதனாலுங் கொலைப்பாவம் வருமென்று கூறிற்று.

257.reading: If there were people who perceived flesh as another creature's wound, it would not be eaten.
257.nuance: பெறின் suggests such perceivers are rare. The commentators stress impurity, yet 'another's wound' can equally appeal to fellow-feeling, as the wound belongs to someone. That second emphasis is my own reading.

258.reading: Those whose vision has parted from fault don't eat flesh that has parted from life.
258.nuance: The two lines mirror each other with தலைப்பிரிந்த: a person parted from defect faces flesh parted from life. Parimelazhagar says they see for themselves that it is a corpse, so no rule is needed.

259.reading: Better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices is not taking one creature's life and eating.
259.nuance: A thousand rites weigh less than one abstention. The commentators treat this as a comparison of merit, but the verse can also be read as a challenge to ritual, and that sharper reading isn't one they give.

260.reading: All living beings fold their hands and worship the one who doesn't kill and has refused flesh.
260.nuance: The beings that have been spared do the worshipping, an image rather than a report. Parimelazhagar insists that the two abstentions are only fruitful together, which closes the loophole of the previous verses.

links.note: 253 uses the weapon-holder as the model of a mind closed to good. 774 celebrates a warrior who plucks a spear from his own body and laughs. The Kural honours in the section on polity the same figure that it distrusts in the section on virtue.
329 condemns killers as base. 256 extends the guilt to the customer who keeps them in business, so the customer can't look down on the butcher.

Both move the worth of sacrifice elsewhere: 88 calls hospitality the வேள்வி that misers miss, and 259 ranks not killing above a thousand sacrifices. The Kural repeatedly tests ritual by how others are treated.

Nearly the same ending: all living beings worship. In 260 the object is one who doesn't kill and doesn't eat flesh; in 268 it is one who has mastered, or on another reading lost, his own self. One route looks outward and the other inward.

source_issues: 253: the verse text reads நன்னூக்காது, where Parimelazhagar's gloss has நன்று ஊக்காது. The readings follow the gloss.
254: the verse text has lost its first letter, ருளல்லது for அருளல்லது.
251, 260: Parimelazhagar's gloss is duplicated in the source.
253, 255: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
259: Kalaignar's entry ends with a stray verse number, 260.
258: Manakkudavar's entry begins with a fragment of the verse text.
